source_text: τὰ δ’ ἑξῆς προςαποδοτέον καὶ τὴν ἐκ τῆς βαρβάρου φιλοσοφίας Ελληνικὴν κλοπὴν σαφέστερον ἤδη παραστατέον. Φασὶ γὰρ σῶμα εἶναι τὸν θεὸν οἱ Στωϊκοὶ καὶ πνεῦμα κατ’ οὐσίαν, ὥσπερ ἀμέλει καὶ τὴν ψυχήν. πάντα ταῦτα ἄντικρυς εὑρήσεις ἐν ταῖς γραφαῖς. μὴ γάρ μοι τὰς ἀλληγορίας αὐτῶν ἐννοήσῃς τὰ νῦν ὡς ἡ γνωστικὴ παραδίδωσιν ἀλήθεια, εἰ ἄλλο τι δεικνύουσαι, καθάπερ οἱ σοφοὶ παλαισταί, ἄλλο μηνύουσιν. ἀλλ’ οἳ μὲν διήκειν διὰ πάσης τῆς οὐσίας τὸν θεόν φασιν, ἡμεῖς δὲ ποιητὴν μόνον αὐτὸν καλοῦμεν καὶ λόγῳ ποιητήν. παρήγαγεν δὲ αὐτοὺς τὸ ἐν τῇ Σοφίᾳ εἰρημένον διήκει δὲ καὶ χωρεῖ διὰ πάντων διὰ τὴν καθαριότητα, ἐπεὶ μὴ συνῆκαν λέγεσθαι ταῦτα ἐπὶ τῆς σοφίας τῆς πρωτοκτίστου τῷ θεῷ. ναί, φασίν, ἀλλὰ ὕλην ὑποτίθενται οἱ φιλόσοφοι ἐν ταῖς ἀρχαῖς, οἵ τε Στωϊκοὶ καὶ Πλάτων καὶ Πυθαγόρας, ἀλλὰ καὶ Ἀριστοτέλης ὁ Περιπατητικός, οὐχὶ δὲ μίαν ἀρχήν. ἴστωσαν οὖν τὴν καλουμένην ὕλην ἄποιον καὶ ἀσχημάτιστον λεγομένην πρὸς αὐτῶν, καὶ τολμηρότερον ἤδη μὴ ὂν πρὸς τοῦ Πλάτωνος εἰρῆσθαι. καὶ μή τι μυστικώτατα μίαν τὴν ὄντως οὖσαν ἀρχὴν εἰδὼς ἐν τῷ Τιμαίῳ αὐταῖς φησι λέξεσιν· νῦν δ’ οὖν τὸ παρ’ ἡμῶν ὧδε ἐχέτω· τὴν μὲν περὶ πάντων εἴτε ἀρχὴν εἴτε ἀρχὰς εἴτε ὅπῃ δοκεῖ τούτων πέρι, τὸ νῦν οὐ ῥητέον, δἰ ἄλλο μὲν οὐδέν, διὰ δὲ τὸ χαλεπὸν εἶναι κατὰ τὸν παρόντα τρόπον τῆς διεξόδου δηλῶσαι τὰ δοκοῦντα. ἄλλως τε ἡ λέξις ἡ προφητικὴ ἐκείνη ἡ δὲ γῆ ἦν ἀόρατος καὶ ἀκατασκεύαστος ἀφορμὰς αὐτοῖς ὑλικῆς οὐσίας παρέσχηται. Ναὶ μὴν Ἐπικούρῳ μὲν ἡ τοῦ αὐτομάτου παρείσδυσις οὐ παρακολουθήσαντι τῷ ῥητῷ γέγονεν ἐντεῦθεν ματαιότης ματαιοτήτων, τὰ πάντα ματαιότης. Ἀριστοτέλει δὲ μέχρι σελήνης ἐπῆλθε καταγαγεῖν τὴν πρόνοιαν ἐκ τοῦδε τοῦ ψαλμοῦ· κύριε, ἐν τῷ οὐρανῷ τὸ ἔλεός σου καὶ ἡ ἀλήθειά σου ἕως τῶν νεφελῶν. οὐδέπω γὰρ ἀποκεκάλυπτο ἡ τῶν προφητικῶν δήλωσις μυστηρίων πρὸ τῆς τοῦ κυρίου παρουσίας. Τάς τε αὖ μετὰ θάνατον κολάσεις καὶ τὴν διὰ πυρὸς τιμωρίαν ἀπὸ τῆς βαρβάρου φιλοσοφίας ἥ τε ποιητικὴ πᾶσα μοῦσα, ἀλλὰ καὶ ἡ Ἑλληνικὴ φιλοσοφία ὑφείλετο. Πλάτων γοῦν ἐν τῷ τελευταίῳ τῆς Πολιτείας αὐταῖς φησι ταῖς λέξεσιν· ἐνταῦθα δὴ ἄνδρες ἄγριοι, διάπυροι ἰδεῖν, παρεστῶτες, καταμανθάνοντες τὸ φθέγμα, τοὺς μὲν ἰδίᾳ παραλαβόντες ἦγον, τὸν δὲ Ἀριδαῖον καὶ τοὺς ἄλλους συμποδίσαντες χεῖράς τε καὶ πόδας καὶ κεφαλήν, καταβαλόντες καὶ ἐκδείραντες, εἷλκον παρὰ τὴν ὁδὸν ἐκτὸς ἐπ’ ἀσπαλάθων κνάπτοντες. οἱ μὲν γὰρ ἄνδρες οἱ διάπυροι ἀγγέλους αὐτῷ βούλονται δηλοῦν, οἳ παραλαβόντες τοὺς ἀδίκους κολάζουσιν· ὁ ποιῶν, φησί, τοὺς ἀγγέλους αὐτοῦ πνεύματα καὶ τοὺς λειτουργοὺς αὐτοῦ πῦρ φλέγον. ἕπεται δὲ τούτοις τὴν ψυχὴν εἶναι ἀθάνατον. τὸ γὰρ κολαζόμενον ἢ παιδευόμενον ἐν αἰσθήσει ὂν ζῇ, κἂν πάσχειν λέγηται.
pass_a_gloss: But the next thing to be restored and the Greek theft from barbarian philosophy to be shown more clearly. For the Stoics say that God is a body and spirit in essence, just as also the soul. You will find all these things clearly in the scriptures. Do not think of their allegories now as the gnosis delivers the truth, if they show something else, just as the ancient wise men, they indicate something else. But they say that God passes through all of existence, we however call Him only the creator and the creator by word. They were led by what was said in Wisdom, 'it passes through and penetrates all things because of its purity', since they did not understand that these things were said about the primal wisdom of God. Yes, they say, but the philosophers hypothesize matter in the beginnings, both the Stoics and Plato and Pythagoras, and also Aristotle the Peripatetic, not however one principle. Let them know therefore the so-called matter, uncreated and unformed, as it is said by them, and more boldly not to be said in relation to Plato. And not having known the most mystical, one truly existing principle in the Timaeus, he says in the same words. Now therefore let our position be as follows: the thing about all things, whether principle or principles or however it seems to them, is not to be said now, because of nothing else, but because it is difficult to show the things that seem according to the present manner of exposition. Besides, the prophetic speech, 'the earth was invisible and unformed', has provided them with opportunities for material existence. For Epicurus, the idea of spontaneity did not follow from what was said, hence vanity of vanities, all things are vanity. And for Aristotle, providence extended up to the moon from this psalm, 'Lord, your mercy and truth reach to the clouds'. For the revelation of prophetic mysteries had not yet been unveiled before the coming of the Lord. The punishments after death and the punishment by fire, as well as all creative muse, but also Greek philosophy, were borrowed from barbarian philosophy. Plato, in the last book of the Republic, says in the same words: 'here indeed wild men, fiery to see, standing, learning the sound, having taken some privately, led them away, but having bound the hands and feet and head of Aridaeus and the others, having thrown them down and flayed them, they dragged them along the road outside, striking them with asphalathoi'. For the wild men, the fiery ones, want to indicate angels to him, who having taken the unjust, punish them; He who makes, he says, His angels spirits and His servants a burning fire. It follows that the soul is immortal. For what is punished or educated, being in sensation, lives, even if it is said to suffer.

pass_b_english: We must now restore what follows and demonstrate more clearly the Greek appropriation of barbarian philosophy. The Stoics claim that God is a body and spirit in essence, just as they also claim the soul is. You will find all these points plainly in the Scriptures. Do not mistake their allegorical interpretations for the truth that the gnosis now delivers, for even if they appear to show something, they actually signal something else, much like the ancient wise wrestlers. They assert that God permeates all existence, but we call Him only the Creator and the Creator by the Word. They were misled by the passage in Wisdom — 'it passes through and penetrates all things because of its purity' — since they did not understand that these words refer to the primordial Wisdom created by God. True, they reply, but the philosophers — Stoics, Plato, Pythagoras, and Aristotle the Peripatetic alike — posit matter as a first principle, not a single one. Let them therefore acknowledge the so-called matter, described by them as unqualified and formless, and even more boldly, as non-being, according to Plato's own statement. And although he knew the most mystical truth — that there is only one truly existing principle — he speaks of it in the Timaeus in those very words. For now, let our position stand thus: the question concerning all things, whether of one principle or many or whatever they suppose about them, is not to be discussed at present, for no other reason than the difficulty of explaining what seems plausible in the present mode of exposition. Besides, that prophetic saying — 'the earth was invisible and unformed' (Genesis 1:2) — has furnished them with a starting point for material substance. In Epicurus's case, the notion of chance arose because he did not attend to the literal sense, resulting in 'vanity of vanities, all is vanity.' As for Aristotle, he limited providence only as far as the moon, drawing from this psalm: 'Lord, your mercy reaches to the heavens, your truth to the clouds' (Psalm 36:6). For the prophetic revelation of mysteries had not yet been unveiled before the Lord's coming. Both the punishments after death and the penal fire were borrowed from barbarian philosophy by the entire poetic tradition, and by Greek philosophy as well. Plato, in the final book of the Republic, puts it in these very words: 'Here are wild men, fiery to behold, standing by, discerning the cry; taking some aside privately, they led them away, but binding Aridaeus and the others hand and foot and head, throwing them down and flaying them, they dragged them along the road outside, beating them with thorns.' He intends the fiery wild men to represent angels who seize the wicked and punish them — 'He makes His angels spirits, His ministers a flame of fire.' It follows from this that the soul is immortal; for that which is punished or corrected, existing in sensation, continues to live, even if it is said to suffer.

review.notes: The translation accurately captures the complex arguments regarding the origins of philosophical concepts in barbarian thought. Pass A preserves the Greek syntax and nuances, while Pass B provides necessary scriptural citations (Genesis 1:2 and Psalm 36:6) which are required by the instructions for inline citations. The translation of 'ἄποιον' as 'unqualified' (Pass B) or 'uncreated' (Pass A) and 'ἀσχημάτιστον' as 'formless' is acceptable within the bounds of patristic translation. The description of the Plato passage in the Republic is faithful to the Greek text.

Stromata 14, paragraph 1: 'ἡ δὲ γῆ ἦν ἀόρατος καὶ ἀκατασκεύαστος' matched with 'the earth was invisible and unformed' (Genesis 1:2). 'κύριε, ἐν τῷ οὐρανῷ τὸ ἔλεός σου καὶ ἡ ἀλήθειά σου ἕως τῶν νεφελῶν' matched with 'Lord, your mercy and truth reach to the clouds' (Psalm 36:6).
